title: Procrastination is a mood problem, not a time problem
description: You do not put things off because you are lazy or disorganised. Research says you are avoiding a feeling — and that changes the cure completely.

body.heading: The real reason we delay
paragraphs: Psychologists who study procrastination, among them Fuschia Sirois and Timothy Pychyl, describe it as a problem of mood regulation: we avoid a task because of how the task makes us feel — bored, anxious, frustrated, unsure — and putting it off repairs the mood for a little while.
That is why time-management tips so often fail. A better diary does not fix a feeling. The delay was never really about the calendar.

body.heading: Work with the feeling, not against yourself
paragraphs: Start by naming the feeling honestly: “This report makes me anxious because it might be judged.” A named feeling is smaller than a vague dread, and it suggests its own remedy — a draft nobody will see, a smaller first piece, a question asked early.

Then shrink the task until the feeling shrinks with it. Five honest minutes of the real thing beats an afternoon of reorganising your desk to avoid it. Self-compassion helps too: people who forgive themselves for a delay are, in studies, less likely to delay the next task.

body.heading: A kinder question
paragraphs: Instead of “why am I so lazy?”, try “what is this task making me feel, and what is the smallest kind way through it?” The first question shames; the second one plans.
You are not a broken machine that needs stricter management. You are a person avoiding an unpleasant feeling — which is the most fixable problem in the world.

takeaway: Procrastination is short-term mood repair, not laziness: name the feeling, shrink the task, and forgive the delay.
